i0: *If* isn't the only word for conditions. English uses ***unless, as long as, provided (that), in case*** and ***even if*** to add different meanings: an exception, a strict condition, a precaution, or *it doesn't matter*.
i1: After all of these, we use a **present** tense for the future, just like after *if*: *I'll come **unless** it **rains**.* For the basic patterns, see [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/).
cup-unless.s: **unless** = *if … not*. Use a **positive** verb after it: *I'll go **unless** it rains* (= if it doesn't rain).
cup-unless.b0: ***Unless*** means *except if* or *if … not*: *You can't come in **unless** you have a ticket.* = You can't come in **if** you **don't** have a ticket.
cup-unless.b1: The verb after *unless* is **positive** in form, but the meaning is negative. Don't add *not*: ***unless** it **rains*** (not *unless it doesn't rain*).
cup-unless.b2: Like *if*, *unless* takes a **present** tense for the future: ***Unless** you **hurry**, you'll miss the bus.*
cup-as-long-as.s: **as long as / provided (that) / providing** = only if: *You can borrow my car **as long as** you're careful.*
cup-as-long-as.b0: These phrases mean ***only if*** or ***on condition that***. They make a strict condition: *You can go out **as long as** you're back by ten.* = You can go out, but only if you're back by ten.
cup-as-long-as.b1: ***Provided (that)*** and ***providing (that)*** mean the same, but they're more formal. ***On condition that*** is very formal: *The loan was approved **on condition that** it was repaid within a year.*
cup-as-long-as.b2: Use a **present** tense for the future: ***As long as** you **work** hard, you'll pass.* Not *as long as you will work*.
cup-as-long-as.w1: provided = only if, not if not
cup-in-case.s: **in case** = because something **might** happen: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* It's different from *if*.
cup-in-case.b0: We do something ***in case*** something happens = as a precaution, because it **might** happen: *I'll take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* (I'll take it now, because it might rain.)
cup-in-case.b1: Compare: *I'll take an umbrella **if** it rains* = I'll only take it if it is raining when I leave.
cup-in-case.b2: Use a **present** tense for the future after *in case*: *in case it **rains*** (not *in case it will rain*). For the past, use the past simple: *I took my coat **in case** it **got** cold.*
cup-in-case.b3: ***In case of*** + noun is used on signs and in formal English: ***In case of** fire, use the stairs.* (= if there is a fire)
cup-in-case.n3: formal: if there is an emergency
cup-in-case.w1: Call only when you're late: if.
x.cup-unless-s01: *Unless* = if … not: if you don't exercise, you won't get fit.
x.cup-as-long-as-s01: Only if you've finished: *as long as*.
q.cup-as-long-as-s02: Which expression is the most formal?
x.cup-as-long-as-s02: *On condition that* is the most formal.
q.cup-in-case-s02: *I'll buy some extra food in case Tom comes.* What does this mean?
